lesson.grammar_point: modals should, could and might for advice

listenings.text: I fly about forty times a year, and there are three things I tell everybody who is going abroad for the first time. The first one is about the carry-on. Anything you cannot replace in twenty-four hours should be in the small bag that goes with you into the plane. Passport, medicine, the charger, and one change of clothes. Big bags get lost, and they usually come back, but not on the day you need them. The second one is money. You should change a little currency before you travel, but not everything, because the rate at the airport is the worst one you will find anywhere. And the third one is the one almost everybody ignores. Check which terminal you are flying from on the morning of the flight, not the week before. Terminals change, the airline knows, and the ticket in your hand does not update itself.

I teach first-year students, and there are two things I say in the first week that nobody believes until much later. The first one is to keep a portfolio from day one, including the work you do not think is good enough. You are the worst judge of your own work at nineteen, and in two years you will look at something you almost threw away and see the beginning of what you do now. The second one is about networking, which is a word most students hate, and I understand why. It sounds like being charming at parties. It is not that. It is being remembered by two or three people who know what you actually do. Two is enough. And the thing they get most wrong is waiting until they are ready to apply for something. There is no such moment. You might not get it, and you find out in an afternoon instead of wondering for a year.
